content:
## Quick Decision Guide

After you receive AI output, you need to decide what to do with it. Use this page as a fast reference for making that call.

## Accept

**Use the output as-is (with minor touch-ups).**

Accept when all of the following are true:

- It answers what you actually asked
- You understand it well enough to explain it
- You've checked for errors and found none (or none that matter)
- The tone, format, and level of detail fit your purpose
- You can take ownership of it — it's genuinely yours now

**Examples of accept-worthy output:**

- A Python function that does exactly what you asked, uses logic you can trace, and handles your expected inputs correctly
- A thesis statement that makes your argument clearly and fits your assignment
- An explanation of a concept that matches what you know from class and fills in the gaps you had
- A CSS layout that works correctly and matches the structure you described

**Watch out for:** Accepting because it *looks* good without checking if it *is* good. Confident, well-written output still needs to be verified.

## Revise

**The core content is useful, but something specific needs to change.**

Revise when:

- The direction is right but specific parts are off
- There are identifiable issues you know how to fix
- The tone, voice, or format needs adjustment
- Something is missing that you can add
- A factual detail or logic issue is fixable without starting over

**Common revision situations:**

| What needs fixing | What to do |
|---|---|
| Tone is too formal / too casual | Rewrite affected sentences to match your register |
| One factual claim is wrong | Correct it using a reliable source |
| Code has a logic error you can identify | Fix the specific lines; test the change |
| A required section is missing | Add it yourself, or use a follow-up prompt for just that piece |
| Variable names or word choices are unclear | Rename them — don't regenerate the whole thing |
| The argument is close but not quite yours | Revise the key sentences to reflect your actual position |

**The revision principle:** Start from your evaluation findings, not from the top. Fix what you identified — don't edit everything just because you're in editing mode.

## Reject

**The output missed badly enough that starting over is faster than fixing it.**

Reject when:

- The AI answered a fundamentally different question
- The errors are so numerous or deep that fixing them would take more effort than rewriting
- The approach is wrong in a way that can't be patched
- The output contains claims you can't verify and don't trust
- After reading it, you still can't understand what it's doing or saying

**Examples of reject-worthy output:**

- Code that uses a completely different approach than what you asked for, making it unusable for your context
- An essay paragraph that argues the opposite of your position
- An explanation that's technically about the right topic but at the wrong level, with no clear way to adjust it
- Output that made so many wrong assumptions that the whole thing is built on a foundation that doesn't apply to your project

**After a reject:** Don't just regenerate with the same prompt. Take a minute to diagnose what went wrong (see Diagnose the Miss), fix the prompt, and generate again. The rejection taught you something — use it.

## The One-Sentence Test

Still not sure which category your output falls into? Try this:

> *"Can I explain what this does, does it match what I asked for, and are there any errors I can't account for?"*

- **All yes** → Accept
- **Mostly yes, with specific fixable gaps** → Revise
- **One or more clear no** → Reject (or revise heavily, which might mean reject)

## Remember

Whichever decision you make — you're the one responsible for what ends up in your final work. Accepting something means you stand behind it. Revising means you've done the work to make it yours. Rejecting means you made a smart call about where your time is best spent.

All three are valid. All three are part of working with AI well.
